text: You already know a security group is a stateful firewall attached to a resource rather than to a subnet's route table. In Azure, that's the Network Security Group, or NSG, and this lesson moves past the generic concept into the exact Azure mechanics: the anatomy of its rules, and the one detail that decides everything about how they're evaluated, which is priority.

Every NSG rule has six parts: a priority number from 100 to 4096, a source and destination, a port, a protocol, and an allow or deny action. Azure evaluates rules in priority order, lowest number first, and stops at the first match. There's no most-specific-rule-wins logic — a priority-100 allow beats a priority-200 deny every single time, no matter which rule looks more specific.

Every NSG also ships with default rules you didn't write, sitting at priority 65000 and above so your own rules can always override them: allow traffic from inside the VNet, allow Azure's own load balancer health probes, and deny everything else inbound. A brand-new NSG with zero custom rules already blocks the internet but lets VMs in the same VNet talk freely — you're adding exceptions on top of a secure baseline, not building one from nothing.

A worked example for a typical web server: priority 100 allows HTTPS on port 443 from the Internet service tag, open to the whole internet. Priority 110 allows SSH on port 22, but only from one specific admin IP address, locking remote management down tight. Everything else falls through to the default deny at 65500 — there's no need to write an explicit deny rule for every other port yourself.

An NSG can attach to a subnet, to a VM's network interface, or to both at once. When both exist, inbound traffic is checked against the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG, and it has to clear both to get through. Most designs keep it simple with one NSG per subnet. Next: giving that web server a public IP and spreading traffic across it with a load balancer.
